title: A New Era of Collaboration for Legal and Professional Services
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the infrastructure and service-delivery thesis and materially develops it through Shared Spaces: a concrete model for extending AI-enabled workflows across firms, clients and internal functions. It also links customer-built workflows to possible business-model change, while stopping short of independently demonstrating security, adoption or service improvements.
qs: These went beyond mere productivity gains and into new ways of working that had the potential to reshape business models.

But AI-powered legal and professional services work has one missing link to be their most effective: bringing their clients, advisors, and cross-functional teams into the same intelligent workspace without compromising security or confidentiality of their most sensitive matters.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source accepts that value comes from redesigned workflows rather than access or individual productivity alone, and materially extends the proposition to secure, cross-organisational workspaces connecting firms, clients and internal functions. Its product and governance claims describe proposed infrastructure and emerging service models, while its reported benefits and exploratory testimonial do not establish realised Shared Spaces outcomes.
qs: These went beyond mere productivity gains and into new ways of working that had the potential to reshape business models.

### Enabling the New Way to Collaborate, Securely  Shared Spaces enables organizations to unlock best-in-class service delivery and greater transparency with secure, shared AI-native environments where internal teams and external partners — whether they are Harvey customers or not — work from the same intelligence.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source accepts the application-layer thesis and materially extends it by presenting Shared Spaces as secure infrastructure for cross-organisational legal workflows and new service-delivery models. Its claims support the cluster’s workflow and service-design analysis, while remaining vendor assertions rather than evidence of durable defensibility or demonstrated outcomes.
qs: But AI-powered legal and professional services work has one missing link to be their most effective: bringing their clients, advisors, and cross-functional teams into the same intelligent workspace without compromising security or confidentiality of their most sensitive matters.
These went beyond mere productivity gains and into new ways of working that had the potential to reshape business models.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led augmentation model and materially extends its operating-model redesign proposition with a concrete cross-organisational workspace linking clients, law firms, advisers and internal teams. It assigns AI document analysis and insight generation to the system while retaining experienced attorneys for strategic counsel, although its claimed benefits rest mainly on prospective use cases and design-partner testimonials rather than quantified outcomes.
qs: Externally, clients bring together their law firms, professional service advisors, and internal teams on the same complex matters.

Harvey's collaborative capabilities represent the future we're building: a platform where we and our clients work together in real-time, where AI accelerates document analysis and insight generation, and where our attorneys apply seasoned expertise to deliver strategic counsel.

st.t: Shared infrastructure: Harvey proposes continuous client collaboration
st.an: The source directly advances the cluster’s principal proposition: Shared Spaces is intended to move legal service delivery beyond isolated productivity gains toward secure, cross-organisational workflows, real-time joint analysis and client collaboration. It also aligns with the synthesis’s caveats because several benefits remain prospective, reported through design partners, and the product was still in early access; lawyer oversight is endorsed but not fully operationally specified.

kp.k: Shared AI workspaces extend collaboration across organizational boundaries
kp.d: Harvey argues that document repositories and communication tools leave a gap in AI-enabled collaboration. Shared Spaces is presented as a shared environment connecting in-house legal, finance, risk and business teams with law firms and professional service advisors, including participants who are not Harvey customers.
qs: But these early innovators also showed us what was missing: a secure way to collaborate across organizational boundaries.

Cross-functional teams can collaborate internally: legal working alongside finance, risk, and business units. Externally, clients bring together their law firms, professional service advisors, and internal teams on the same complex matters.

kp.k: Custom workflows support new service models and self-service
kp.d: Harvey reports that customers had already built custom workflows and bespoke client solutions before Shared Spaces, describing business-model reshaping as potential rather than an established result. Proposed shared-workspace applications include cross-border due diligence, regulatory policy updates and self-service NDA review for clients or internal business partners.
qs: Law firms built custom workflows to deliver new service models. Professional service networks created bespoke solutions to add value collaboratively with clients.
These went beyond mere productivity gains and into new ways of working that had the potential to reshape business models.
Cross-border M&A transactions where deal teams across time zones collaboratively build due diligence analysis in Vault
Self-serve NDA review for clients or cross-functional partners through custom Workflows

kp.k: Cross-organizational collaboration requires granular access controls and auditability
kp.d: Harvey presents confidentiality, security and governance as necessary conditions for sharing sensitive transactions and privileged communications. It reports adding resource-level permissions and logs of security-critical actions since opening access in December; these are vendor descriptions of product capabilities.
qs: We've designed Shared Spaces knowing we're handling the most sensitive matters organizations face — from confidential M&A deals to privileged attorney-client communications.
We've strengthened governance controls with granular permissions that let you control access at the resource level.
We've enhanced audit capabilities with comprehensive logs that track every security-critical action — from granting access to publishing content within a space.

kp.k: Integrated teamwork could refocus counsel on strategic advice
kp.d: The article describes Deutsche Telekom and Gleiss Lutz as exploring integrated collaboration on complex regulatory matters. Deutsche Telekom's Claudia Junker frames integrated internal and external legal teamwork as a future capability. Gleiss Lutz partner Ralf Morshäuser says joint due diligence and contract work enables greater focus on strategic advice and negotiation.
qs: Deutsche Telekom and Gleiss Lutz are exploring how Harvey transforms collaboration on complex regulatory matters, moving from parallel workstreams to integrated teamwork.

Harvey empowers our legal team – nationally and internationally – and external counsel including Gleiss Lutz to work more efficiently as one integrated unit in the future, tackling intricate challenges together while maintaining the rigor and security our global operations demand.

Harvey allows us to collaborate more effectively — whether we're jointly working on due diligence or refining complex contracts — so we can focus our expertise where it truly matters: high-end strategic advice and negotiation.

kp.k: Real-time visibility challenges sequential professional-service deliverables
kp.d: In testimonials carried by Harvey, PwC's Russell Taylor describes shared analysis as allowing clients to act on advice immediately rather than await final reports. IFS's Andrew Binstead reports visibility into developing analysis and reasoning, with corporate development, advisors and legal counsel collaborating on outputs. These are customer accounts of changing delivery relationships, not quantified outcome findings.
qs: This transparency and shared capability means our clients benefit from our advice immediately, not weeks later in a final report. It's a new model for professional services.
With Shared Spaces, we can see analysis as it develops, understand reasoning, and collaborate on the outputs together.
We're all working from the same intelligence, whether it's our corporate development team, advisors like PwC, or our law firms.

kp.k: Collective learning and shared analysis underpin envisioned client value
kp.d: KWM's Michelle Mahoney describes Harvey's evolution from productivity software into client collaboration and argues that lawyers learning from one another changes legal work and improves client outcomes. IAG's Anna Golovsky anticipates real-time joint analysis and more efficient use of external expertise. IAG's account is explicitly forward-looking rather than a measured efficiency result.
qs: Harvey is evolving from a legal productivity tool to a collaborative platform with our clients.

When you create opportunities for lawyers to learn from each other and share experiences in open, accessible forums, you fundamentally change how legal work gets done which delivers better outcomes for clients.
Our teams will be able to collaborate alongside external counsel in real-time, analysing data together, building insights collectively and harnessing external expertise more efficiently.

kp.k: Practitioner-guided AI supports rather than replaces legal judgment
kp.d: Thompson Hine's Bill Garcia envisions AI accelerating document analysis and insight generation while experienced attorneys supply strategic counsel and rigorous legal thinking. Flex's Melissa Zujkowski describes exploration of shared workspaces across operations in 30 countries, emphasizing potential capabilities conditional on maintaining transparency and control.
qs: Harvey's collaborative capabilities represent the future we're building: a platform where we and our clients work together in real-time, where AI accelerates document analysis and insight generation, and where our attorneys apply seasoned expertise to deliver strategic counsel.
Collaborative AI workspaces, guided by experienced practitioners, are how we deliver on that expectation.

Operating across 30 countries, we're exploring how Harvey's collaborative workspaces could fundamentally change how we handle legal complexity, moving from siloed work streams to shared environments where our internal teams and external counsel collaborate from the same intelligence.

kp.k: Reported benefits include capacity growth without additional headcount
kp.d: Harvey cites its recent RSGI report: more than 50% of law firms report improved client service, 82% of legal teams report increased capacity without added headcount, and 55% of in-house teams report reimagining law-firm collaboration. The document supplies no sample size, study period or methodology, and presents these as reported benefits of Harvey generally, not measured effects attributable specifically to Shared Spaces.
qs: According to our recent RSGI report, more than 50% of law firms say Harvey improves client service through faster delivery and better quality work.
On the in-house side, 82% of legal teams report increased capacity without adding headcount.
And 55% of in-house teams say Harvey is helping them reimagine collaboration with their law firms, opening new conversations about how legal work is delivered and shared.

kp.k: Early-access deployment precedes planned broader collaboration capabilities
kp.d: The February 19, 2026 article distinguishes existing early access from expected general availability in March. Harvey also describes continued investment in collaboration analytics, intelligent notifications and workflow customization; these are development intentions rather than established customer outcomes.
qs: We're continuing to invest in the capabilities that enable even deeper, multiplayer collaboration: advanced analytics that surface insights about how teams are working together, intelligent notifications that keep everyone aligned without overwhelming them, and richer customization that lets organizations tailor spaces to their specific workflows and needs.
Shared Spaces is live in early access with organizations around the world, with general availability expected in March.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey Team claims AI is moving beyond individual productivity toward shared service delivery and potentially different business models.
pts.d: The author says customers had already built custom workflows and bespoke client solutions before Shared Spaces. It presents Shared Spaces as the missing cross-organizational workspace, supporting joint due diligence, regulatory-policy updates and self-serve NDA review. Claims of secure collaboration rest on permissions, access controls, auditability and governance; they are product claims, not independently demonstrated security findings in this document.

pts.k: Deutsche Telekom and Gleiss Lutz speakers describe more integrated client–counsel work and greater scope for strategic legal advice.
pts.d: Deutsche Telekom GC Claudia Junker anticipates national and international legal teams working more efficiently with external counsel on regulatory matters. Gleiss Lutz partner Ralf Morshäuser says joint due diligence and contract work allow lawyers to concentrate expertise on high-end advice and negotiation. These are named partner/client accounts and expectations, without quantified results.

pts.k: PwC and IFS speakers claim shared AI workspaces replace delayed reporting and opaque engagements with immediate advice and visible, collaborative analysis.
pts.d: PwC TMT Deals Partner Russell Taylor describes a new professional-services model in which clients see deal issues as advisors find them rather than waiting for a final report. IFS corporate-development executive Andrew Binstead reports visibility into developing analysis and reasoning, with legal counsel able to join the same workspace. These claims concern professional-services and transaction engagements, not solely legal work. Taylor explicitly situates Harvey within a broader collaboration-technology suite.

pts.k: KWM and IAG speakers predict collective learning and real-time client–counsel analysis will improve outcomes and use external expertise more efficiently.
pts.d: KWM Chief Innovation Officer Michelle Mahoney characterizes Harvey as evolving from a productivity tool into a client collaboration platform and links shared lawyer learning to better client outcomes. IAG legal-operations executive Anna Golovsky describes future joint analysis and collective insight-building with external counsel. The stated benefits are qualitative and partly prospective.

pts.k: Thompson Hine and Flex speakers envision faster AI-assisted analysis and integrated global work while retaining experienced legal judgment and client control.
pts.d: Thompson Hine Chief Practice Innovation Officer Bill Garcia describes AI accelerating document analysis and insight generation while attorneys supply strategic counsel and rigorous legal thinking. This is an augmentation model guided by experienced practitioners, not a claim of autonomous lawyer replacement. Flex litigation executive Melissa Zujkowski describes exploration of shared workspaces across a business operating in 30 countries, with potential benefits rather than established global outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The quantitative basis is a cited RSGI report on reported Harvey benefits; the collaboration claims also rely on design-partner testimonials and product descriptions.
pts.d: Harvey Team attributes three figures to its recent RSGI report: more than 50% of law firms report improved client service, 82% of in-house teams report increased capacity without additional headcount, and 55% report reimagined law-firm collaboration. These are reported experiences concerning Harvey broadly, not identified measurements of Shared Spaces specifically. The document provides no sample size, survey dates, methodology, quantified time savings or independent outcome assessment. The named organizations are explicitly design partners; their statements mix present-tense experience with aspirations and exploration.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The February 19, 2026 article combines existing customer practices and early-access experience with near-term rollout expectations and undated future benefits.
pts.d: The author says access opened in December, implying December 2025, and that general availability is expected in March, implying March 2026. Existing custom workflows predate Shared Spaces. Some partner statements describe present benefits, while Deutsche Telekom, IAG, Thompson Hine and Flex explicitly discuss future or exploratory use. Further analytics, notifications and customization are investment plans without delivery dates. Effective collaboration is framed as requiring shared access across organizations without compromising confidentiality, supported by granular permissions and audit controls; external participants need not already be Harvey customers.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes primarily affect enterprise legal departments, external law firms, professional-services advisors and corporate cross-functional teams.
pts.d: For law firms, the claimed effects are faster and better client delivery, closer collaboration and more focus on strategic advice. For in-house legal teams, they are greater capacity without added headcount and more visibility and control over external work. For professional-services advisors, represented by Big Four firm PwC, the change is immediate shared analysis rather than sequential reporting. Corporate development, finance, risk and business units can participate alongside lawyers. Harvey is the software vendor enabling these arrangements, not an ALSP delivering the legal work. The document does not claim job losses, staffing-ratio changes, pricing changes or access-to-justice benefits for underserved individuals.
